title: Where each clock gets its time
caption: Physical clocks take their time from hardware and NTP; causal metadata advances only from events and messages. A hybrid logical clock is where the two meet: it takes physical time as an input and merges received timestamps like a logical clock.

title: Lamport counters across two nodes
caption: Each send carries the sender's incremented counter, and each receive jumps past it. The two counters differ, but every receive is numbered after the send that caused it.

title: Two costs of one algorithm
caption: Input size drives both kinds of cost. Each growth class describes how time can grow as N grows; Big-O states an upper bound on that growth, not a measured speed.

title: What an indexed lookup still has to do
caption: An index finds where the matches start, but the query still visits each of the K matches and may fetch table columns for each one. The cost grows with K as well as with log N.

title: What Little's Law counts
caption: Little's Law counts everything inside the measured boundary: requests waiting for capacity as well as requests being served. Mean time in the system starts at admission and ends at departure.

title: Concurrency past the knee
caption: Adding concurrency raises throughput only until a resource saturates. Beyond that point extra work waits in queues: throughput flattens and then falls while latency climbs.

title: Where the throughput ceiling sits
caption: A cache hit avoids the database; a miss still needs it. If the database is the limiting resource, adding app servers cannot raise throughput past it.

title: Who constructs, who depends
caption: The feature depends only on the cart contract it owns; the composition boundary decides which implementation fulfils it. Transport details stay behind the adapter, so changing them does not ripple into checkout.

title: Tangled modules and a narrow seam
caption: Left: every module reaches into its neighbours, so one change can ripple through all four. Right: Cart and Checkout meet only at an interface, so each can change behind it.

title: A shallow copy shares its list
caption: copy() creates a second Company, but both still point at one MutableList. A change through either reference is visible through both: a shallow copy is not an immutable snapshot.

title: Racing writers versus shared values
caption: With shared mutable state, a writer and a reader race on the same object. With immutable state, readers share one value safely and a change produces a new object; publishing that new reference still needs its own rule.

title: Only the representation crosses the network
caption: Serialization flattens an in-memory object into bytes another runtime can read; deserialization rebuilds a separate object on the other side. Only the agreed representation crosses the network.

title: An old reader meets new bytes
caption: Treat received bytes as untrusted input. An older reader decodes within size and schema limits, validates meaning, and turns anything malformed, incompatible or invalid into a controlled error or a supported fallback.

title: A blocking read parks its thread
caption: A blocking read() holds its thread until data arrives. The kernel can run other threads meanwhile, but this one stays parked with its stack allocated.

title: One thread, many descriptors
caption: One thread registers interest in many descriptors, waits in poll(), and runs the callback for whichever descriptor is ready before returning to poll() again.

title: Thread-per-request
caption: Thread-per-request: each request occupies its own thread for the whole I/O wait, so concurrent waits need as many threads.

title: Event loop
caption: Event loop: one thread waits on many pending operations and runs a short callback whenever one completes. A slow callback delays every other completion.

title: M:N coroutines
caption: M:N scheduling: many coroutines share a small pool of N OS threads. A coroutine that suspends releases its thread for another; a blocking call inside one still occupies the thread.

title: Producers, a buffer and two workers
caption: Producers enqueue at their own pace; workers dequeue and flush to the backend at theirs. The queue absorbs bursts, but with two workers, items can finish out of order.

title: End-to-end backpressure
caption: The slow sink's limit travels upstream one stage at a time until the source slows down. If any stage ignores it, work piles up at that stage instead.

title: TCP flow control
caption: The receiver advertises how much buffer space it has left. At window 0 the sender stops and waits; a later window update lets it resume.

title: A policy at every boundary
caption: Each boundary can have its own buffer policy: drop the oldest pending events before parsing, bound enrichment work, and conflate before rendering so only the latest value waits.

title: Admission for a source that cannot wait
caption: A callback source cannot be suspended, so admission must be explicit: try a bounded offer, and when the queue is full, reject, replace or persist according to the contract. The consumer's free capacity decides what is admitted next.

title: Read path with a cache
caption: A hit returns straight from the cache. A miss reads the source of truth, fills the cache, then returns the value.

title: Write, then invalidate
caption: Write the source of truth first, then invalidate the cache entry, so the next miss reloads the committed value.

title: The stale-fill race
caption: A reader that fetched v1 before the writer committed v2 can store v1 after the invalidation. Version checks or leases reject that late fill.

title: Caches between a user and the data
caption: Each layer can answer a request before it reaches the next. A miss falls through towards the database, whose buffer pool is itself a cache of disk pages.

title: Protecting the source when the cache fails
caption: When the cache misses or fails, a miss budget decides how much load reaches the authoritative store. Requests over budget are rejected explicitly or served a permitted stale value instead of overwhelming the source.

title: Pure transitions, separate effects
caption: The transition function only computes the next state and the effects it requests. A separate runner performs logging, network calls and timers, which keeps the transition pure and testable.

title: The loop around a state machine
caption: Every source feeds one queue, transition() turns each event into the next state, and observers of the stored state can trigger the next events.

title: Four states and their events
caption: Four states and the events that move between them. An event with no arrow from the current state is ignored; that is a deliberate policy of this machine.

title: Ignoring a stale completion
caption: Serializing events through one owner lets it compare every completion with the current request ID. A late failure for attempt A is ignored because attempt B is current; only valid events change state or request work.

title: One event, independent subscribers
caption: The publisher emits one OrderPlaced event without calling each module. Analytics, Inventory and Notification each receive it independently, but all still depend on the event's schema and delivery contract.

title: A command, a recorded outcome and a fact
caption: The command asks the payment owner to act; the event reports what happened. Recording the outcome and the intent to publish together lets publication recover after a crash, and subscribers receive the fact independently.

title: Failover to a secondary
caption: After the primary crashes, the client's next request goes through the load balancer to the secondary. Requests in flight during the crash still need their own retry and idempotency rules.

title: Circuit breaker states
caption: A circuit breaker stops calling a failing dependency once failures exceed its threshold, waits out a reset timeout, then lets a probe decide whether to close again or reopen.

title: Bulkheads still share resources
caption: Separate admission budgets stop a slow search dependency from using up the payments path. Both paths still share CPU, memory and connection capacity, so those need budgets too.

title: Redundancy and its shared dependencies
caption: Redundant app servers sit behind a health-checking load balancer; the primary database replicates to two replicas, and the cache can fall back to a replica. Each copy covers some failures, while the primary still needs tested promotion.
